opus-5.5.text:
I think tactile sensing is one of those things that's both underrated and, in a way, overrated at the same time, depending on who you ask.

On one hand, if you look at how humans manipulate objects, touch is absolutely essential. There are these classic studies where people's fingertips are anesthetized, and suddenly simple tasks like striking a match or picking up a small object become incredibly clumsy. Vision tells you where things are and roughly what's going on, but the moment you make contact, a lot of the critical information — how much force you're applying, whether the object is slipping, the friction, the compliance of the material — is really only available through touch. So for contact-rich tasks like insertion, in-hand manipulation, handling deformable or fragile objects, tactile feedback carries information that vision alone just can't give you, especially when the hand itself is occluding the contact point.

On the other hand, I think we have to be honest about where the field is right now. A lot of the recent progress in robot learning, the large-scale imitation learning and the foundation-model-style policies, has been driven almost entirely by vision plus proprioception. And these systems can do surprisingly dexterous things. Part of the reason is that vision can implicitly infer a lot about contact, and part of it is that the policies learn to compensate. So the question isn't really "is tactile data useful?" because it clearly is. The question is "when does it become the bottleneck, and how do we make it scalable?"

And that's where the challenges come in. Tactile sensors are still fairly heterogeneous. There's no standard form factor like there is with cameras. They can be fragile, they drift, they're hard to calibrate, and the data from one sensor often doesn't transfer to another. Simulating touch realistically is also very hard, so we can't easily lean on simulation the way we do for vision. And critically, it's hard to collect tactile data at scale, because when a human teleoperates a robot, the human usually doesn't feel what the robot feels. So the demonstrations don't necessarily reflect good tactile-driven behavior.

So my view is that tactile data is going to be really important, especially as we push toward more fine-grained, contact-rich, human-level dexterity. But to unlock it, we need progress on a few fronts together: better and more standardized hardware, ways to collect demonstrations where the human actually has access to touch feedback, for example through wearable devices or haptic teleoperation, and learning methods that can fuse touch with vision in a way that knows when to rely on which modality. I see it less as a replacement for vision and more as the missing piece for the last mile of manipulation, the part where things are in contact and precision really matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think tactile data is one of those things that's easy to underrate, because so much of the progress in robot learning over the past few years has been driven by vision. Cameras are cheap, there's an enormous amount of visual data in the world, and we've gotten very good at training models on it. So the natural instinct is to just push harder on vision and hope it covers everything.

But manipulation is fundamentally about contact. The moment you grasp something, the most important information about what's happening is at the fingertips, and that's exactly where cameras tend to fail you. Your own hand occludes the object. You can't see how much force you're applying, whether the object is starting to slip, whether you've made contact with a surface or you're still a millimeter above it. Humans deal with this effortlessly. There are classic experiments where people's fingertips are anesthetized and they suddenly struggle with things like striking a match or buttoning a shirt, even though their vision is perfectly intact. That tells you something about how much of dexterity lives in touch.

So from a learning perspective, I see tactile sensing as filling in the part of the state that vision structurally can't observe. For a lot of tasks, you can get away without it. Pick and place on a tabletop, you can mostly do with cameras. But as soon as you move toward fine-grained, in-hand manipulation, dealing with deformable things, inserting a connector, handling something fragile, the policy needs feedback from contact, and without it you end up with brittle behaviors that work in demos and break in the real world.

The challenge, and the reason it hasn't taken off the way vision has, is that tactile data is hard to collect and hard to standardize. Every sensor has a different form factor and output. The sensors wear out. And critically, there's no internet of touch. You can't scrape it. So the question I find interesting isn't just whether tactile matters, it's how we get enough of it, and how we integrate it with the large vision and language models that are driving the rest of the field. I think things like teleoperation setups that capture touch alongside vision, or ways of transferring human tactile experience to robots, are going to be important there. My view is that the robots that end up being genuinely dexterous will be the ones that learned to feel, not just to see.

astra-6.text:
I think tactile data is important because manipulation is fundamentally about contact. Vision can tell a robot where an object is and help it plan how to approach it. But once it makes contact, it needs to understand what’s happening: Is the grasp stable? Is the object slipping? Is it applying too much force?

Imagine picking up a paper cup. You need enough pressure to hold it, but you don’t want to crush it. Touch gives you feedback that can be difficult to get from a camera, especially when your hand is blocking the view.

The challenge is turning those signals into useful actions. Collecting tactile data is one part; learning how to use it alongside vision and movement is another. I see touch as a complementary source of information that can help robots adjust during an interaction, rather than relying entirely on what they predicted before making contact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think tactile data is really important because manipulation is fundamentally about contact. Vision can tell a robot where an object is and help it plan a grasp, but once it touches the object, it needs to understand what’s happening at that contact. Is the object slipping? How much force is it applying? Has a part actually seated into place? Those things can be difficult to infer from images alone.

Imagine picking up a paper cup. You need enough force to hold it, but you don’t want to crush it. Touch gives you feedback to adjust your actions as you go, especially when the object’s properties aren’t known in advance.

The challenge is turning tactile signals into something a robot can learn from and generalize across objects and tasks. So I see touch as complementary to vision and proprioception. Together, they can give robots a much richer understanding of their physical interactions.
